title: Taxes on Investments
description: Gains, dividends, basis, and the year that changes the rate in the example.
wolfLine: The gain is the sale minus the basis. The year decides which rate this example uses.

capital-gain.definition: Profit from selling an investment for more than your cost basis. Held a year or less, it is short-term. Held more than a year, it is long-term.
capital-gain.example: Bought at $2,000, sold at $2,600. The gain is $600.

cost-basis.definition: What you paid for an investment, including commissions you cannot ignore. The gain is the sale minus this number.
cost-basis.example: Eight shares at $25 each have a cost basis of $200.

lessons.title: A Capital Gain
lessons.summary: The profit is the sale minus what you paid.

steps.title: Two prices
steps.body:
A [[capital gain]] is the sale price minus your [[cost basis]]. Bought at **$2,000**, sold at **$2,600**, the gain is **$600**.

A loss is the same math when the sale is lower. This unit is education, not a reason to buy or sell.

steps.prompt: What is the gain on a $2,000 purchase sold for $2,600?
The same investment is sold for $1,700. What is the loss?
What is cost basis, in this example?
steps.explain: Basis is what you paid. The sale is what you received.

steps.prompt: A gain is taxed as if the whole sale price were profit.
steps.explain: Only the $600 above the $2,000 basis is the gain.

lessons.title: Short or Long
lessons.summary: More than a year changes the rate in this example.

steps.title: Eleven months, or a year and a day
steps.body:
Held a year or less, the **$600** gain is short-term and taxed as ordinary income. This example puts it in a **22%** ordinary rate, so the tax is **$132**.

Held more than a year, it is long-term. This example uses a stated **15%** long-term rate, so the tax is **$90**. The 0%, 15%, and 20% cutoffs depend on income. This lesson does not invent those cutoffs. Waiting saves **$42** in this example.

steps.prompt: The $600 short-term gain is taxed at the stated 22%. What is the tax?
The $600 long-term gain is taxed at the stated 15%. What is the tax?
How much less tax is the long-term result in this example?
Selling after 11 months gets the long-term rate.
steps.explain: Eleven months is a year or less. Long-term means more than a year.

lessons.title: Dividends
lessons.summary: Qualified is not the same word as ordinary.

steps.title: Two names on the form
steps.body:
A dividend is a payment from a stock or a fund you still hold. **Qualified** dividends can be taxed at the long-term rates. **Ordinary** dividends are taxed as ordinary income.

In this example, **$400** of qualified dividends at a stated **15%** cost **$60**. **$100** of ordinary dividends at a stated **22%** cost **$22**. Not every dividend is qualified.

steps.prompt: What is 15% of $400 of qualified dividends, at that stated rate?
What is 22% of $100 of ordinary dividends, at that stated rate?
What is the tax on both dividends in this example?
Every dividend is qualified and taxed at the long-term rate.
steps.explain: Ordinary dividends are taxed as ordinary income. The form tells you which is which.

lessons.title: Cost Basis
lessons.summary: The shares remember what you paid.

steps.title: Count the shares
steps.body:
Eight shares at **$25** each have a [[cost basis]] of **$200**. Sold at **$40** each, the proceeds are **$320**. The [[capital gain]] is **$120**.

Reinvested dividends can raise the basis. Ignoring them makes the gain look bigger than it is.

steps.prompt: What is the cost basis of 8 shares at $25?
What are the proceeds of those 8 shares at $40?
What is the gain?
The gain is $320, because that is what the buyer paid you.
steps.explain: The gain is $120. The other $200 is your own basis coming back.

lessons.title: Tax-Loss Harvesting
lessons.summary: A loss can cancel a gain. A quick buyback can cancel the loss.

steps.title: Net them
steps.body:
Tax-loss harvesting means selling an investment that is down so the loss can offset a gain. A **$500** gain and a **$200** loss leave a **$300** net gain.

A wash sale can disallow the loss if you buy the same investment within **30 days** before or after the sale. This is the common rule, at a high level. It is not a trading plan.

steps.prompt: A $500 gain and a $200 loss. What is the net gain?
How much of the $500 gain did the loss offset?
steps.explain: The loss is $200, so $200 of the gain is offset.

steps.prompt: What can disallow the loss?
choices: Buying the same investment back within 30 days
Waiting more than a year to sell
Keeping the shares and never selling
steps.explain: That quick buyback is the wash-sale problem. Holding is not a sale, so there is no loss to claim yet.

steps.prompt: A loss you have not sold is a deduction this year.
steps.explain: The loss is real on paper only until you sell. Unsold shares have not produced a deductible loss.

lessons.title: Why the Year Matters
lessons.summary: Same gain. The rate on this pair is the whole difference.

steps.context: Both pages are the same **$600** [[capital gain]]. The holding period is the only change.

lessons.title: Interest, Even If You Leave It
lessons.summary: Form 1099-INT does not wait for a withdrawal.

story.title: Elena’s savings interest
story.body:
Elena is 44 and a teacher. Her savings account paid **$80** of interest. She left it in the account.

The bank will report it on Form 1099-INT. The **$80** is taxable even though she did not withdraw it. It is not a [[capital gain]]. She did not sell anything.

She also still holds a fund. Unsold, it has no gain to report this year, whatever the screen says it is “worth.”

steps.prompt: How much interest did the savings account pay?
steps.explain: The story’s figure is $80.

steps.prompt: Why is the $80 taxable this year?
choices: Interest is income when it is paid, even if it stays in the account
Interest is a long-term capital gain
steps.explain: Leaving it in the account does not defer it. A sale is a different event.

steps.prompt: The unsold fund produces a capital gain this year because the price went up on the screen.
steps.explain: The gain waits for a sale. An unsold fund is still hers.

steps.prompt: Which form reports the bank interest?
steps.explain: 1099-INT is the interest form. The W-4 is withholding. Schedule C is a business.

steps.prompt: Interest left in the account is still ___.
steps.explain: Taxable. The withdrawal is not what makes it income.

lessons.title: A Brokerage 1099
lessons.summary: Read the gain from two lines, not from their sum.

steps.title: Four different facts
steps.body:
Proceeds **$2,600**. [[Cost basis]] **$2,000**. Qualified dividends **$400**. Interest **$80**.

Adding all four lines is not a tax. The gain is proceeds minus basis.

doc.title: Brokerage summary
doc.subtitle: These lines are not one total

doc.title: Brokerage summary

steps.prompt: What is the interest on this page?
steps.explain: The interest line is $80.

doc.title: Brokerage summary

steps.prompt: Qualified dividends are $400. At a stated 15% rate, what is the tax on that line alone?
steps.explain: $400 × 0.15 = $60. That rate is the example’s stated rate, not a cutoff this page computed.

steps.prompt: The four lines should be added together and called the gain.
steps.explain: The gain is $600. Dividends and interest are their own income.

steps.prompt: Cost basis is $900. The sale is $1,200. What is the gain?
A $1,000 short-term gain is taxed at a stated 24%. What is the tax?
A sale after 400 days is still short-term.
steps.explain: More than a year is long-term. 400 days is more than a year.

steps.prompt: Interest of $50 posted to a savings account and left there is:
steps.explain: It is interest income for the year it was paid.
